t.1.122.1: Then, O king, the mighty Bhāradvāja, having approached Drupada, said to the son of Pṛṣata, "Know me as your friend."
t.1.122.2: Drupada said: Your understanding is immature, brahmin, and not at all fitting, since you forcefully tell me, O twice-born, "I am your friend."
t.1.122.3: For never, O fool, is there friendship between exalted kings and men such as these, bereft of fortune and fallen from wealth.
t.1.122.4: Even friendships wear away with time for those who grow old. Formerly I did have a friendship with you, a bond founded on our equal capacity.
t.1.122.5: Never at any time in this world is friendship seen to be ageless: desire draws it apart, or anger cuts it down.
t.1.122.6: Do not cling thus to a worn-out friendship; form a new friendship instead. Best of the twice-born, my friendship with you was bound up with a purpose.
t.1.122.8: Friendship and marriage are proper between two whose wealth is equal and whose lineage is equal, but not between one who is prosperous and one who is impoverished.
t.1.122.7: A poor man is no friend to a rich man, nor an unlearned man to a learned one; a coward is no friend to a hero. Why is a former friendship sought?
t.1.122.10: Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus addressed by Drupada, the mighty Bhāradvāja, overwhelmed with anger, reflected for a moment.
t.1.122.9: One unversed in the Veda is no friend to one versed in the Veda, nor is one without a chariot a friend to a chariot-warrior; one who is not a king has no fellowship with a king. Why then is a former friendship desired?
t.1.122.11: Having resolved in his mind concerning the Pāñcāla king, the wise one went to the city of the foremost of the Kurus, the city named after the elephant.
t.1.122.12: Then the princes, having come out together from Gajasāhvaya, roamed about there joyfully, those heroes, playing with a vīṭā.
t.1.122.13: Then, while they were playing, the ball fell into a well, and they could not find any way to recover the ball.
t.1.122.14: Then the mighty Droṇa, seeing those princes in need of help, smiled gently out of kindness and addressed them.
t.1.122.16: This handful of reeds has been charged by me with a mantra through a magic weapon. Behold its power, which no other possesses.
t.1.122.15: Ah, shame on your kṣatriya strength, and shame on this mastery of weapons of yours, you who, born in the lineage of Bharata, fail to retrieve the ball!
t.1.122.18: The princes saw that, their eyes wide open with amazement, and having looked at the ball that had been retrieved, they spoke to the one who had pierced the ball.
t.1.122.17: I shall pierce the ball with a blade of grass, then that blade with another, and that one with yet another; by such a chain joined together I will lay hold of the ball.
t.1.122.20: Describe me to Bhīṣma by my appearance and by my qualities; he, being of very great wisdom, will at once recognize me.
t.1.122.19: We salute you, O brahmin; this skill is not found in others. Who are you? As whom should we know you? What may we do for you?
t.1.122.21: Saying "So be it," they all went and told Bhīṣma, their grandfather, the brahmin's words exactly as spoken, and of that extraordinary feat.
t.1.122.22: Having heard the princes' account, Bhīṣma recognized that this was Droṇa, and reflected thus: "He is indeed a fitting teacher."
t.1.122.23: Then Bhīṣma, best of weapon-bearers, having himself brought him there and honored him well, questioned him closely about the reason for his coming, and Droṇa told him all of it.
t.1.122.25: As a celibate student, self-disciplined and wearing matted hair, I dwelt there a very long time, for many years, out of the desire to master the science of archery.
t.1.122.24: Formerly, O steadfast one, I went to the great seer Agniveśya to obtain weapons, out of a desire to master the science of archery.
t.1.122.26: Now the son of the king of the Pāñcālas, the mighty Yajñasena, pursued his studies together with me, toiling diligently and attentively in the service of our teacher.
t.1.122.27: There he was my friend, helpful and dear to me. Alas, keeping company with him, I took delight for a very long time, O Kauravya, from childhood on, and we studied together as well.
t.1.122.28: Approaching me there, he, who did what was pleasing and spoke kindly, addressed me thus, O Bhīṣma, with words that increased my affection:
t.1.122.30: The kingdom shall be yours to enjoy, friend; I swear to you by the truth. My pleasures, my wealth and my comforts shall all be at your disposal.
t.1.122.29: Droṇa, I am the dearest son of my great-souled father; when that Pāñcāla king consecrates me in the kingship, then
t.1.122.32: Greatly delighted, I went again to my dear friend, now established in his kingdom, remembering our former companionship and those words of his.
t.1.122.31: Thus addressed, he departed. And I, having mastered the weapons and longing for wealth, heard that he had been consecrated as king, and thought, “I have attained my goal.”
t.1.122.34: But when I had come before him and approached him as a friend, Drupada, laughing at me as if I were a worthless nobody, spoke these words.
t.1.122.33: Then, O lord, I approached Drupada, my former friend, and said to him, 'O tiger among men, know me to be your friend.'
t.1.122.36: For never, O dull-witted one, is there friendship between exalted kings and men such as these, bereft of fortune and stripped of wealth.
t.1.122.35: This understanding of yours is crude, brahman, and hardly fitting, that you so boldly say to me, 'I am your friend,' O twice-born.
t.1.122.37: One who is not versed in the Veda is no friend to one who is, one without a chariot is no friend to a chariot-warrior, and one who is not a king is no friend to a king either. Why then is a former friendship sought?
t.1.122.38: Thus addressed by Drupada and overwhelmed with anger, I came to the Kurus, O Bhīṣma, desiring pupils endowed with virtues.
t.1.122.40: "They are your disciples," he said, O king, and gave them to Droṇa according to the prescribed rite; and that great archer accepted the Kauravas as his disciples.
t.1.122.39: Bhīṣma, together with the sons of Pāṇḍu, received him as their teacher, bringing along all those grandsons and riches of many kinds.
t.1.122.42: A certain task that I long for turns over and over in my heart; once you have mastered the weapons, that must be given to me by you. Speak the truth about this, O sinless ones.
t.1.122.41: Having accepted them all as pupils, Droṇa, pleased at heart, then spoke these words in private, alone, to those who had respectfully approached him.
t.1.122.43: Hearing that, the Kauravas fell silent, O lord of the people; but then Arjuna, scorcher of foes, promised to accomplish it all.
t.1.122.44: Then, smelling Arjuna's head again and again and embracing him with affection, he wept for joy.
t.1.122.45: Then the mighty Droṇa made the sons of Pāṇḍu master weapons of many kinds, both divine and human.
t.1.122.46: Likewise other princes, O bull of the Bharatas, having assembled, then approached Droṇa, best of the twice-born, for the sake of weapons: the Vṛṣṇis and the Andhakas, and kings from various lands.
t.1.122.47: Rādheya, the son of the sūta, also came at that time to Droṇa as his teacher. But the sūta's son, vying with Pārtha and exceedingly intolerant, relied on Duryodhana and held the Pāṇḍavas in contempt.
